nodes.ask: Headache in the ED. First moves?
options: Airway and vital signs, GCS, a neurologic exam with the fundi; time the onset and screen red flags
Non-contrast CT head before any history or exam; take the story once the report is back
IV morphine for the pain first, then a full history and neurologic exam once it has settled
Metoclopramide and ketorolac at triage; examine and take the history only if they fail
nodes.chainStep: Airway, breathing and vital signs; GCS and a neurologic exam with fundoscopy; establish the rate of onset and time to peak; screen for red flags
nodes.why: Stability comes first: the Canadian CVT guideline, for example, starts with airway, breathing and circulation and looks for raised intracranial pressure, fundoscopy included. Then the red flags choose the route. NICE CG150 lists, among others, a sudden onset reaching maximum intensity within 5 minutes, worsening headache with fever, a new neurological deficit, impaired consciousness, head trauma in the past 3 months and symptoms of giant cell arteritis, and adds compromised immunity and a cancer that spreads to the brain. NICE NG228 asks for the rate of onset and the time to peak, the fundi look for papilledema, and the pressure screens for malignant hypertension (180 systolic or 120 diastolic or more). Imaging before the history skips the questions that choose the scan, opioids sedate and change the pupils of the patient being examined, and treating first leaves the red flags unasked.
nodes.note: Not in this version: children, post-dural puncture headache, acute angle-closure glaucoma, pituitary apoplexy, cervical artery dissection and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction. A seizure with headache goes to the seizure pathway.

outcomes.if: Depressed consciousness, no fever; GCS below 13 or the airway at risk
Thunderclap, GCS 13 or more; peak within 5 minutes, no deficit, no fever
Fever; with neck stiffness, a rash, confusion, or no other source found
New focal deficit; sudden weakness, speech or field loss, not vision loss with GCA features
Another red flag; GCS 13 or more, afebrile, no focal deficit, not a thunderclap
No red flags; normal exam, a primary headache pattern
Over 50 with GCA features; a new headache with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms, vision loss included
Papilledema; BP below 180/120, not pregnant
Others at home are ill too; headache and nausea around a fuel-burning appliance
BP over 180/120 with confusion; or visual change, not pregnant
BP over 180/120, no organ damage; alert, normal fundi and neurological exam, not pregnant

Another secondary-cause flag; over 50 without GCA features, cancer, low immunity, head injury in 3 months, an anticoagulant, a worsening or changed pattern, a cough or exertion trigger, new cognitive change, or unexplained vomiting
Worse upright, better lying
Pregnant or postpartum; a new headache unlike her usual, no household cluster

nodes.ask: Depressed consciousness, no fever. First?
options: Airway, capillary glucose, then an immediate non-contrast CT head
Lumbar puncture first, to look for blood or infection in the CSF
MRI brain first, since it shows more than CT
nodes.chainStep: Protect the airway; capillary glucose; immediate non-contrast CT head; ask witnesses how it started
nodes.why: NICE NG128 excludes hypoglycemia as the cause of sudden neurological symptoms. Reduced consciousness is one of the signs of subarachnoid hemorrhage in NICE NG228, and a GCS below 13 calls for an immediate non-contrast CT in suspected stroke (NG128). NG228 diagnoses SAH on the CT and turns to an LP only when the CT is clear; in meningitis guidance an abnormal level of consciousness is one of the findings that put a CT before any LP, because a mass lesion can herniate after a tap. NG128 asks for an immediate non-enhanced CT, not an MRI first. When the patient cannot describe the onset, ask a witness, without delaying the scan. How to secure the airway is not in the sources read.

sources.where: CT before lumbar puncture (text before Table 2)

orders.dose: Exclude hypoglycemia
Secure it when the patient cannot protect it; the method and the intubation threshold are not in the sources read

outcomes.if: Subarachnoid blood; blood in the subarachnoid space
Intracerebral hemorrhage; blood in the brain tissue
A subdural, mass, abscess or hydrocephalus
No bleed, no mass; CT clear

orders.dose: COHb, pH and lactate

nodes.ask: Thunderclap headache, GCS 13 or more, no deficit. Next?
options: Urgent non-contrast CT head, with senior review
Lumbar puncture now; CT only if the tap is bloody
Treat as migraine; scan only if the pain does not settle
MRI brain as an outpatient this week
nodes.chainStep: Senior review; urgent non-contrast CT head (most accurate within 6 hours of onset); effective analgesia, opioids if needed
nodes.why: A thunderclap headache, typically peaking within 1 to 5 minutes, is a red-flag symptom of subarachnoid hemorrhage. NICE NG228 asks for urgent senior review and an urgent non-contrast CT, whose accuracy is highest within 6 hours of onset, and the ACR rates a non-contrast CT usually appropriate for a sudden severe headache and MRI usually not appropriate. Most thunderclap headaches are not SAH, migraine among the other causes, but that should not deter investigation, and the LP comes only after a clear CT.

orders.dose: Effective relief, including opioids if needed; record them, since they sedate and change the pupils

outcomes.if: Subarachnoid blood; diagnose SAH
Clear, within 6 hours; done under 6 hours from onset, reported by a radiologist
Clear, after 6 hours; done more than 6 hours from onset

nodes.ask: Clear CT within 6 hours of onset, reported by a radiologist. Next?
options: Senior review; LP for xanthochromia at 12 hours or more if SAH is still suspected
Discharge home without further assessment, since the CT has ruled out SAH
Start enteral nimodipine and admit under neurosurgery for angiography
Catheter angiography of the head before any other test or review
nodes.chainStep: Clear CT within 6 hours: senior review and specialist advice on other causes; if SAH is still suspected, LP for xanthochromia at least 12 hours after onset (NICE does not offer it routinely after a radiologist-reported scan)
nodes.why: NICE NG228: when a CT done within 6 hours of onset and reported by a radiologist shows no SAH, do not routinely offer an LP; think about alternative diagnoses, discuss with a senior and seek specialist advice. Such a scan has a high diagnostic accuracy, but it does not end the assessment, so discharge without that review is wrong. Nimodipine is for a confirmed SAH, and catheter angiography is rated usually not appropriate as the first study for a sudden severe headache.
nodes.note: Exam note: many US question banks still expect an LP after any negative CT. The key keeps the LP for doubt that remains, at least 12 hours after onset, so both answers sit inside it.

outcomes.if: No other cause, no remaining doubt; exam normal, headache settling
Doubt remains; LP done at least 12 hours after onset
A venous cause suspected; estrogen, postpartum, or worse lying flat

nodes.ask: Clear CT done more than 6 hours after onset. Next?
options: Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset; spectrophotometry for xanthochromia
Discharge with analgesia: a clear CT at this stage has ruled out SAH
Admit and repeat the non-contrast CT head in 24 hours to look for blood
Outpatient MRI of the brain within the week, then decide on a lumbar puncture
nodes.chainStep: Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset; spectrophotometry for xanthochromia
nodes.why: After 6 hours the CT is less accurate and false negatives are more likely, so NICE NG228 says to consider an LP, done at least 12 hours after onset, when enough bilirubin has formed to be detected reliably; xanthochromia on spectrophotometry diagnoses SAH. A clear late CT does not rule SAH out. The next test NG228 names is the LP, not a repeat scan, and the ACR rates MRI usually not appropriate as the first study for a sudden severe headache.

outcomes.if: Xanthochromia; raised bilirubin on spectrophotometry
No xanthochromia; LP 12 hours or more after onset

nodes.ask: Subarachnoid hemorrhage confirmed. Next?
options: CT angiography of the head now; urgent call to the neurosurgical center
Tranexamic acid now, then a routine catheter angiogram later in the week
MRI and MR angiography tomorrow, then refer if an aneurysm shows
Admit to a general ward, analgesia, and repeat the CT head in 24 hours
nodes.chainStep: CT angiography of the head without delay; urgent discussion with the neurosurgical center; analgesia, opioids if needed
nodes.why: NICE NG228 offers CT angiography of the head without delay to find the cause and guide treatment, and an urgent discussion with a specialist neurosurgical center, because the risk of rebleeding is highest within 24 hours of onset. ESO recommends against routine antifibrinolytic drugs before the aneurysm is treated, and NICE says tranexamic acid must not delay treatment to secure it. Waiting a day for an MRI or a repeat CT spends the highest-risk window.

orders.dose: Effective relief, including opioids if needed
Not routinely before the aneurysm is treated, and never a reason to delay securing it

outcomes.if: Aneurysm; the blood pattern fits its rupture
No cause found; an aneurysm is still suspected
Aneurysm, pattern does not fit rupture; the blood pattern is not compatible with that aneurysm

nodes.ask: Ruptured aneurysm on CT angiography. While the team plans treatment?
options: Enteral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours; coil or clip the aneurysm early if intervention is an option
Hold treatment of the aneurysm for 2 weeks, until the vasospasm window has passed
Magnesium sulfate infusion in place of nimodipine; secure the aneurysm next week
Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours, injecting the capsule contents IV if swallowing is unsafe
nodes.chainStep: Nimodipine 60 mg by mouth or tube every 4 hours for 21 days, started within 96 hours; if intervention is an option, secure the aneurysm at the earliest opportunity, coiling, or clipping if coiling is not suitable
nodes.why: Nimodipine is given enterally, 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days, starting as soon as possible within 96 hours of the bleed; when the patient cannot swallow, the capsule contents go into an oral syringe and down a nasogastric tube. They must never be injected: deaths, cardiac arrest and cardiovascular collapse have followed. ESO recommends oral nimodipine and recommends against magnesium sulfate. When intervention is an option, the aneurysm is secured at the earliest opportunity, because rebleeding risk is highest in the first 24 hours: NICE offers endovascular coiling, or clipping if coiling is not suitable, and ESO suggests treatment within 24 hours. Holding it for 2 weeks leaves that risk running.

orders.dose: 60 mg (two 30 mg capsules) every 4 hours for 21 consecutive days, started as soon as possible within 96 hours of onset; unable to swallow: capsule contents drawn into an oral syringe, given by nasogastric tube or PEG
Never inject the capsule contents IV or by any parenteral route
30 mg every 4 hours, with close monitoring of blood pressure and heart rate
Endovascular coiling, or clipping if coiling is not suitable, at the earliest opportunity; ESO suggests within 24 hours when the most dedicated team is available

orders.item: Blood pressure before the aneurysm is secured
orders.dose: ESO suggests lowering very high pressure before the aneurysm is secured, slowly, without undershoot, with short-acting drugs (expert opinion; effect on outcome unclear)

Not stated in the text read: NG228 gives no acute target; ESO prose reports only observational targets (120 plus or minus 20, 160, 140 or less) under PICO 1b Additional information; its PICO 1b recommendation boxes are images not yet read

nodes.ask: Suspected giant cell arteritis. Next?
options: ESR and CRP, and start glucocorticoids now; confirm with biopsy or imaging
ESR and CRP, but hold glucocorticoids until the temporal artery biopsy is done
ESR and CRP, and start glucocorticoids only if the ESR comes back raised
Non-contrast CT head first; start glucocorticoids only if it shows a cause
nodes.chainStep: ESR and CRP; start glucocorticoids without delay; urgent specialist referral; temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound to confirm
nodes.why: With a strong clinical suspicion, EULAR starts glucocorticoids without delay while the confirmatory tests are pending and refers urgently; headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual disturbance raise that suspicion. ESR and CRP are typically raised in GCA and both are normal in under 3%, so they support the diagnosis but do not gate the first dose. Starting steroids first does not spoil the confirmation: imaging and biopsy can still show GCA weeks into treatment, and the ACR asks for the biopsy within 2 weeks.

orders.dose: Urgent: within 24 hours of presentation, immediately with cranial symptoms
Typically raised in GCA; both normal in under 3%

outcomes.if: Visual loss or amaurosis fugax
No visual or neurological symptoms

nodes.ask: Suspected GCA with visual loss. Glucocorticoid?
options: Pulse IV methylprednisolone, then high-dose oral prednisone
Prednisone 10 mg daily, raised if the biopsy is positive
No steroids: vision already lost will not come back
Tocilizumab alone, to spare an older patient the glucocorticoids
nodes.chainStep: Pulse IV methylprednisolone (ACR: 500 to 1000 mg daily for 3 to 5 days), then high-dose oral prednisone; ophthalmology as soon as possible
nodes.why: For new GCA with threatened vision, the ACR conditionally recommends pulse IV glucocorticoids over high-dose oral; EULAR says pulsed methylprednisolone could be considered for acute vision loss, though its benefit is unclear, and arranging it should not delay oral treatment. Delaying glucocorticoids when vision is affected is the strongest risk factor for permanent blindness, low-dose prednisone is not induction therapy, and tocilizumab is used together with glucocorticoids, not instead of them.

orders.dose: 500 to 1000 mg IV daily for 3 to 5 days, or equivalent
0.25 to 1.0 g IV daily for up to 3 days could be considered; benefit unclear
New visual symptoms: seen as soon as possible by an ophthalmology team

nodes.ask: Suspected GCA, no visual or neurological symptoms. Glucocorticoid?
options: High-dose oral prednisone daily, started today
Prednisone 10 mg daily, raised if the biopsy is positive
Alternate-day prednisone to limit side effects
No steroids until the biopsy result is back
nodes.chainStep: High-dose oral prednisone daily, started today (EULAR 40 to 60 mg/day; ACR high dose up to 1 mg/kg, max 80 mg)
nodes.why: Without cranial ischemia, the ACR prefers high-dose oral glucocorticoids over pulse IV and over moderate doses, given daily rather than on alternate days. EULAR starts 40 to 60 mg/day prednisone-equivalent and tapers to 15 to 20 mg/day within 2 to 3 months, and with a strong suspicion it does not wait for confirmation. A low dose is not induction therapy.

orders.dose: 40 to 60 mg/day; taper to 15 to 20 mg/day within 2 to 3 months, aiming to stop within 12 to 18 months
1 mg/kg up to 80 mg daily, or equivalent; daily, not alternate days
orders.note: The ACR's high-dose definition reaches above EULAR's 40 to 60 mg/day starting range.

nodes.ask: Glucocorticoids started. How is GCA confirmed?
options: Temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks, or ultrasound where there is expertise
Stop the steroids for a week so the biopsy is not falsely negative
A response to steroids confirms it; no biopsy or imaging needed
Temporal artery biopsy after 6 weeks, once the steroids have settled it
nodes.chainStep: Temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids (unilateral, longer than 1 cm), or temporal artery ultrasound where there is expertise
nodes.why: EULAR confirms GCA by imaging or biopsy findings, so a response to steroids is not the test. The ACR conditionally prefers a unilateral temporal artery biopsy longer than 1 cm, within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids, and calls biopsy the optimal approach in the United States; EULAR 2018 accepts ultrasound or MRI of the cranial arteries as well as histology. The steroids are not stopped for the biopsy, since imaging and biopsy can still show GCA weeks into treatment.

orders.dose: Unilateral first, a long segment over 1 cm, within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids
EULAR accepts it; the ACR prefers biopsy in the US, where ultrasound expertise is less common

outcomes.if: Arteritis confirmed

orders.dose: ACR: with oral glucocorticoids for newly diagnosed GCA (conditional); EULAR: tocilizumab or upadacitinib considered, especially for relapsing or refractory disease or a high risk of glucocorticoid harm
Baseline MR or CT angiography of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis

outcomes.if: Negative biopsy; suspicion still high

nodes.ask: Papilledema or a suspected venous thrombosis. Imaging?
options: MRI with MR venography, or CT with CT venography, now
Lumbar puncture first; image only if the pressure is high
Non-contrast CT alone; a clear scan rules out venous thrombosis
D-dimer first; image only if it is raised
nodes.chainStep: Brain imaging with venography now: MRI with MR venography, or non-contrast CT with CT venography
nodes.why: Suspected cerebral venous thrombosis needs parenchymal and venous imaging immediately after stabilization: CT with CT venography, or MRI with MR venography, contrast-enhanced preferred. A non-contrast CT alone cannot rule it in or out, and a D-dimer should not decide whether to image. With papilledema, the UK IIH consensus asks for MRI within 24 hours (CT if MRI is not available) and makes CT or MR venography mandatory; the LP comes only after normal imaging. The ACR rates venography 'may be appropriate' for papilledema and in pregnancy.

orders.dose: Measure it with papilledema: malignant hypertension is 180 systolic or 120 diastolic or more
Confirm papilledema; acuity, pupils, intraocular pressure, perimetry, dilated fundoscopy
CBC, electrolytes, aPTT and INR, creatinine and eGFR, glucose, ALT, TSH, and a pregnancy test if able to become pregnant

orders.item: Venography contrast in pregnancy or the peripartum period
orders.dose: The sources disagree; see the note
orders.note: ACR Variant 6 rates MRV with IV contrast usually not appropriate, and MRV without contrast and CT venography may be appropriate; CSBPR 1.2.1.ii and iii prefer contrast-enhanced CT or MR venography and do not recommend time-of-flight MR venography.

outcomes.if: Venous sinus thrombosis
Clear, papilledema confirmed; no thrombosis, no mass
Clear, no papilledema; no thrombosis, no mass
A mass or hydrocephalus

nodes.ask: Cerebral venous thrombosis on venography. Treatment?
options: Therapeutic LMWH now, even if there is a venous hemorrhage
No anticoagulation while there is blood on the scan
Systemic IV alteplase to dissolve the clot, then anticoagulation
Endovascular thrombectomy as the first-line treatment
nodes.chainStep: Therapeutic-dose LMWH (or IV heparin) as soon as possible, even with intracranial blood; stroke unit care; an oral anticoagulant once stable, for at least 3 months
nodes.why: Therapeutic LMWH or IV unfractionated heparin starts as soon as possible after the diagnosis, LMWH preferred for most, and intracranial or subarachnoid blood is not a contraindication. Systemic thrombolysis is not recommended, and endovascular therapy is not routine first-line treatment; it may be considered when the patient deteriorates despite optimal medical therapy.

orders.dose: Therapeutic dose, subcutaneous; the agent and dose are not stated in CSBPR
Bolus then infusion by institutional protocol; mainly for severe renal impairment or a planned procedure
Avoid heparin; involve hematology

orders.item: A DOAC as the first agent
orders.dose: Not routinely without a parenteral lead-in; case by case only
Not recommended
Treat acute symptomatic seizures; no prophylactic antiseizure drugs
Visual symptoms or raised-pressure signs: urgent ophthalmology, ideally within 24 to 48 hours
Escalated by the papilledema's response; the starting dose is not stated in CSBPR
Endovascular therapy may be considered on deterioration despite optimal medical therapy; decompressive hemicraniectomy for life-threatening mass effect
Warfarin (INR 2.0 to 3.0) or a DOAC once stable, for at least 3 months; at least 3 to 6 months after a major transient risk factor such as the early postpartum period
No DOAC while breastfeeding
Therapeutic LMWH, with thrombosis or obstetric medicine follow-up; no DOAC or warfarin

nodes.ask: Papilledema; brain imaging and venography show no cause. Next?
options: Lumbar puncture lying on the side: opening pressure, then CSF protein, glucose and cells
Lumbar puncture sitting upright: opening pressure, then CSF protein, glucose and cells
Discharge with acetazolamide: normal imaging means no lumbar puncture is needed
Start anticoagulation for a presumed venous thrombosis the venogram missed
nodes.chainStep: Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position, legs extended: opening pressure; CSF protein, glucose and cell count
nodes.why: After normal imaging, everyone with papilledema has an LP to measure the opening pressure and check the contents, lying on the side, relaxed, with the legs extended. The diagnostic criteria use an opening pressure above 25 cm CSF, read with the rest of the picture rather than alone. Normal imaging does not explain papilledema, and with the venography clear there is no thrombosis to treat.

outcomes.if: Over 25 cm CSF; contents normal
25 cm CSF or less; contents normal

nodes.ask: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, vision not declining. Treatment?
options: Weight management if BMI is over 30, acetazolamide, and ophthalmology follow-up
Serial lumbar punctures to keep the pressure down, with ophthalmology follow-up
A long course of oral prednisolone with acetazolamide, and ophthalmology follow-up
A CSF shunt now for the headache, then weight management and follow-up
nodes.chainStep: Weight management (BMI over 30); acetazolamide titrated up; short-term NSAID or acetaminophen (paracetamol), no opioids; ophthalmology follow-up by papilledema grade
nodes.why: Weight loss is the only disease-modifying therapy in typical IIH, and everyone with a BMI over 30 is counselled at the earliest opportunity; acetazolamide could be prescribed for symptoms, though the trial benefit was modest. Serial LPs are not recommended, a prolonged course of steroids is not recommended because of weight gain, and CSF diversion is generally not recommended for headache alone. If vision declines, the acute treatment is surgical.

orders.dose: A popular start is 250 to 500 mg twice a day, titrated up; the IIHTT maximum was 4 g daily
Short-term NSAID or acetaminophen; no opioids; warn about medication overuse
Surgical: CSF diversion or optic nerve sheath fenestration; a lumbar drain can bridge to surgery
Counsel women about side effects and teratogenic risk

nodes.ask: Suspected carbon monoxide poisoning. First moves?
options: 100% oxygen by tight-fitting mask with a reservoir now; COHb on a blood gas
Room air is enough: the pulse oximeter reads 99%; COHb on a blood gas
Pulse CO-oximetry first; start oxygen only if the reading is raised
Analgesia for the headache, then home to rest once the pain has settled
nodes.chainStep: 100% oxygen at once, whatever the SpO2; COHb, pH and lactate on a blood gas; ECG and troponin; neurological exam; find the source and alert the fire service
nodes.why: If CO poisoning is suspected, 100% oxygen starts immediately whatever the saturation, because ordinary pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin. A blood gas measures COHb, pH and lactate. A negative CO-oximetry reading, or even a normal COHb, does not rule it out when the history and symptoms fit. Symptomatic patients are admitted, and the source is found so that no one else is poisoned.

orders.dose: 12-lead ECG and troponin (with CK and CK-MB) in everyone with suspected CO poisoning
In everyone with symptoms
Determine it, and alert the fire department to check the scene

outcomes.if: Severe signs or pregnant; impaired consciousness, seizure, acidosis, respiratory failure, cardiac ischemia, an extremely high COHb, or pregnancy
No severe signs, not pregnant; COHb raised but not extreme, or normal after oxygen on the way in

nodes.ask: Carbon monoxide poisoning with severe signs or in pregnancy. Next?
options: Hyperbaric oxygen within 6 hours; 100% oxygen until then
100% oxygen, stopped as soon as the COHb is back to normal
Hyperbaric oxygen tomorrow, but only if symptoms are still present
nodes.chainStep: Call the hyperbaric center now: HBOT within 6 hours, three sessions in 24 hours; 100% oxygen until then; ECG and troponin monitoring
nodes.why: The German S2k guideline gives HBOT to adults with signs of severe poisoning, including continued impaired consciousness, metabolic acidosis, respiratory insufficiency or cardiac ischemia, and in pregnancy. It should start within 6 hours and is not recommended after 24. Oxygen continues until COHb is normal and the patient is symptom-free, because symptoms do not track COHb clearance.
nodes.note: Not every society in the S2k group agreed: DGINA and DGIIN give HBOT or high-flow normobaric oxygen case by case, because a long-term neurocognitive benefit of HBOT over normobaric oxygen is unclear. S2k gives no number for extremely high; the 25% (15% in pregnancy) US threshold is not in the sources read.

orders.dose: Adults (18 and over), ought to, 78% consensus: within 6 hours, not after 24; three sessions within 24 hours, the first at 300 kPa for 90 minutes, the second and third at 2.4 bar or more
100% until COHb is below 3% and the patient is symptom-free
Warn every patient about the risk, symptoms and timing

nodes.ask: BP over 180/120 with confusion. Before the BP plan?
options: Non-contrast CT head now, while the IV agent is prepared
No imaging: the fundi already show it is hypertensive
MRI brain tomorrow, once the pressure is down
Lumbar puncture to exclude a subarachnoid bleed first
nodes.chainStep: Non-contrast CT head now to exclude a hemorrhage or infarct, which have their own BP targets
nodes.why: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline handles a hypertensive emergency with an acute intracerebral hemorrhage or ischemic stroke in its cerebrovascular section, so a bleed or infarct changes the target; the ACR rates a non-contrast CT usually appropriate for a headache with a neurologic deficit. The fundi cannot show a bleed or an infarct, and waiting for an MRI or doing an LP first leaves the target unset.

outcomes.if: No bleed or infarct; CT clear or PRES-type edema
A bleed or infarct

nodes.ask: BP over 180/120 with encephalopathy, not pregnant. BP plan?
options: ICU, titratable IV agent: systolic down no more than 25% in hour 1, then to 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours
ICU, titratable IV agent: bring the pressure to normal within the first hour, then hold it there
ICU, titratable IV agent: systolic below 120 within the first hour, then hold it there
Oral amlodipine in the department, then discharge to clinic follow-up within a week
nodes.chainStep: ICU with continuous monitoring; titratable IV agent; systolic down by no more than 25% in hour 1, to below 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours, then 130 to 140 over 24 to 48 hours
nodes.why: For a hypertensive emergency without a compelling condition, the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline admits to an ICU and lowers systolic pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, then to under 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours, then cautiously to 130 to 140 over 24 to 48 hours. Rapid correction to normal can cause organ hypoperfusion through lost autoregulation; under 120 in the first hour is the target for aortic dissection; and oral treatment with discharge is for severe hypertension without acute organ damage.
nodes.note: Acute intracerebral hemorrhage, ischemic stroke and pregnancy have their own targets in the guideline; a bleed or infarct on imaging goes to the stroke pathway.

orders.dose: Start 5 mg/h; increase by 2.5 mg/h every 5 minutes to a maximum of 15 mg/h
Start 1 to 2 mg/h, doubling every 90 seconds until BP nears target, then smaller increases every 5 to 10 minutes; maximum 21 mg/h, 72 hours
0.3 to 1.0 mg/kg (max 20 mg) slow IV every 10 minutes, or 0.4 to 1.0 mg/kg/h infusion up to 3 mg/kg/h; not with reactive airway or obstructive pulmonary disease

nodes.ask: A secondary-cause red flag without a specific pattern. Imaging?
options: Brain imaging now: non-contrast CT, or MRI
No imaging: treat as migraine and review in clinic
Lumbar puncture before any imaging
nodes.chainStep: Brain imaging now: non-contrast CT head, or MRI head
nodes.why: NICE CG150 says to consider further investigation of a headache after head trauma in the past 3 months, with compromised immunity or with a cancer that can spread to the brain, and the ACR rates non-contrast CT, MRI, or MRI with and without contrast usually appropriate for a headache with cancer, immunocompromise, onset after 50 or onset after trauma. Treating it as migraine skips that, and in meningitis guidance an immunocompromised state is one of the findings that put a CT before an LP, because a mass lesion can herniate after a tap.

sources.where: CT before lumbar puncture (text before Table 2)

nodes.note: Anticoagulation is not on the CG150 or ACR lists read; it is here as a bleeding risk, and a bleed on an anticoagulant is reversed in the stroke pathway. Over 50 without GCA features, GCA still stays possible.

outcomes.if: A bleed, mass or abscess
No abnormality
New hypertension after 20 weeks; over 140/90 with proteinuria or another new organ sign, such as severe headache or visual scotomata

orders.dose: New hypertension over 140 systolic or 90 diastolic after 20 weeks, with new proteinuria or other new maternal organ dysfunction (severe headaches or persistent visual scotomata included) or uteroplacental dysfunction
Systolic 160 or more or diastolic 110 or more is severe hypertension in pregnancy and is treated urgently; the agent and dose table is reprinted from ACOG and is not shown here

outcomes.if: BP normal, no proteinuria; a venous thrombosis to exclude
Migraine; throbbing, light-sensitive, like previous attacks, oral treatment failed or not tolerated
Tension-type; bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate
Cluster; one-sided orbital pain, red watery eye, restless
Medication overuse; worse on triptans, opioids or combination drugs 10 or more days a month, or simple analgesics 15 or more, for 3 months

nodes.ask: Migraine, no red flags, and treatment at home has failed. In the ED?
options: IV metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, with an IV NSAID such as ketorolac
IV hydromorphone with an antiemetic, repeated until the pain settles
Non-contrast CT head first, then IV treatment once it is reported clear
nodes.chainStep: IV metoclopramide or prochlorperazine plus an IV NSAID (ketorolac); sumatriptan SC if pain persists and nothing rules it out; no opioids
nodes.why: When oral treatment fails, NICE CG150 considers a non-oral metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, adding a non-oral NSAID or triptan if not already tried, and an antiemetic is worth giving even without nausea. Opioids and ergots are not offered for migraine, and people with a migraine diagnosis are not sent for neuroimaging solely for reassurance; the ACR rates imaging usually not appropriate for a primary migraine with a normal exam.
nodes.note: The 2025 AHS assessment of parenteral ED treatment (read in abstract only; the full text was not openly accessible) rates IV prochlorperazine must offer; IV metoclopramide, IV ketorolac and SC sumatriptan should offer; IV dexamethasone may offer; IV hydromorphone must not offer.

nodes.ask: Tension-type headache, no red flags. Treatment?
options: Aspirin, acetaminophen or an NSAID; no opioid
Codeine with acetaminophen
Sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously
Non-contrast CT head before any treatment
nodes.chainStep: Aspirin, acetaminophen or an NSAID (no aspirin under 16); no opioids; no imaging for reassurance; warn about medication overuse
nodes.why: NICE CG150 considers aspirin, acetaminophen or an NSAID for acute tension-type headache and does not offer opioids. Sumatriptan injection is indicated for migraine and cluster headache, and only once that diagnosis is clear. Imaging solely for reassurance is not offered, and the risk of medication overuse headache is explained to anyone using acute treatments.

nodes.ask: Cluster headache attack. Acute treatment?
options: 100% oxygen at 12 L/min or more by non-rebreather, and/or sumatriptan 6 mg SC
Oral sumatriptan tablets, with a second tablet if the pain returns
IV ketorolac with an antiemetic, then reassess the pain
IV morphine titrated to the pain, with oxygen only if saturation falls
nodes.chainStep: 100% oxygen at 12 L/min or more by non-rebreathing mask with reservoir, and/or sumatriptan 6 mg SC; verapamil for the bout with specialist advice; home oxygen
nodes.why: NICE CG150 offers oxygen and/or a subcutaneous or nasal triptan: 100% oxygen at 12 litres a minute or more through a non-rebreathing mask with a reservoir bag. Sumatriptan injection is indicated for cluster headache at a single 6 mg dose. Acetaminophen, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots and oral triptans are not offered for an acute cluster attack.

orders.dose: 100%, at least 12 L/min, non-rebreathing mask with a reservoir bag; arrange home and ambulatory oxygen
6 mg SC; a second 6 mg only after at least 1 hour and some response; max 12 mg in 24 hours

Ischemic coronary disease or coronary vasospasm, Wolff-Parkinson-White or another accessory pathway, prior stroke or TIA, hemiplegic or basilar migraine, peripheral vascular or ischemic bowel disease, uncontrolled hypertension, an ergot or another 5-HT1 agonist within 24 hours, an MAO-A inhibitor within 2 weeks, severe hepatic impairment
Consider for prevention during the bout; seek specialist advice, including on ECG monitoring, if unfamiliar; the dose is not in CG150
Discuss neuroimaging with a headache specialist or neurologist; the ACR rates MRI head with and without contrast usually appropriate

nodes.ask: Medication overuse headache. Management?
options: Stop all overused acute drugs abruptly for at least 1 month; warn it worsens first; consider prophylaxis; review in 4 to 8 weeks
Taper the overused drugs slowly over 3 months; warn it worsens first; consider prophylaxis; review in 4 to 8 weeks
Admit for inpatient withdrawal before any trial at home; consider prophylaxis; review in 4 to 8 weeks
Switch to a different daily acute analgesic; warn it worsens first; consider prophylaxis; review in 4 to 8 weeks
nodes.chainStep: Withdraw all overused acute headache drugs abruptly for at least 1 month; warn that the headache worsens first, with close follow-up; consider prophylaxis for the underlying headache; review at 4 to 8 weeks
nodes.why: NICE CG150 treats medication overuse headache by withdrawing the overused drugs: stop all overused acute headache medicines for at least 1 month, abruptly rather than gradually, and warn that symptoms are likely to get worse before they improve. Prophylaxis for the underlying primary headache is considered alongside, and the diagnosis is reviewed 4 to 8 weeks after withdrawal starts. Inpatient withdrawal is not offered routinely; it is considered for strong opioids, relevant comorbidities or repeated failed attempts. A different daily acute drug is still an acute drug taken daily, not withdrawal.

orders.dose: Not routinely; consider specialist referral or inpatient withdrawal for strong opioids, relevant comorbidities or repeated unsuccessful attempts
Close follow-up and support while symptoms worsen; review the diagnosis 4 to 8 weeks after withdrawal starts

nodes.summary: Fever with neck stiffness, a rash or confusion: suspected bacterial meningitis. Continue in the sepsis and fever pathway, which covers the antibiotics, dexamethasone and when an LP is safe. Antibiotics within 1 hour; when a CT or the LP is delayed, blood cultures, dexamethasone and antibiotics come first.
A new focal deficit or an intracerebral hemorrhage: continue in the stroke pathway, which covers imaging, anticoagulant reversal and blood pressure.

Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: CT angiography, an urgent call to the neurosurgical center, analgesia including opioids, enteral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days, no routine antifibrinolytic, and the aneurysm secured at the earliest opportunity, by coiling, or clipping if coiling is not suitable.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage ruled out: a radiologist-reported CT within 6 hours of onset, or a later CT followed by an LP without xanthochromia. Think about the other causes of a sudden severe headache; they are outside this pathway's sources.

CT angiography shows an aneurysm, but the subarachnoid blood pattern is not compatible with its rupture. Seek specialist opinion without delay from an interventional neuroradiologist and a neurosurgeon.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage with no cause on CT angiography: with an aneurysm still suspected, NICE considers digital subtraction angiography, or MR angiography if DSA is contraindicated, and thinks about other diagnoses if neither shows one. Enteral nimodipine is considered for any confirmed SAH, and neurosurgical advice continues.
Giant cell arteritis confirmed: high-dose glucocorticoids tapered to 15 to 20 mg/day within 2 to 3 months, tocilizumab with them considered, and baseline imaging of the large vessels.

Negative temporal artery biopsy with GCA still suspected: the ACR adds noninvasive imaging of the large vessels to the clinical assessment, and a contralateral biopsy is also appropriate. The glucocorticoid decision stays with the specialist team. With high clinical probability, a provisional diagnosis of GCA may be made, then confirmed or revised during follow-up.

Cerebral venous thrombosis: therapeutic LMWH (or IV heparin) at once, even with intracranial blood; no systemic thrombolysis; seizures treated, not prevented; ophthalmology for visual or raised-pressure signs; then an oral anticoagulant for at least 3 months, at least 3 to 6 months after a major transient risk factor such as the early postpartum period, with no DOAC while breastfeeding.

Venography and brain imaging clear, no papilledema: no venous thrombosis and no mass. The other causes of the headache are outside this pathway's sources; specialist advice continues. If consciousness is still depressed, a BP over 180/120 or a raised COHb sends the patient to those steps; a CT more than 6 hours after onset can still miss a SAH.

A subdural, mass, abscess, hydrocephalus or bleed on imaging: outside this pathway; neurosurgical review now. Anticoagulant reversal is covered in the stroke pathway for an intracerebral hemorrhage only; reversal for a subdural is not in the sources read.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension with vision not declining: weight management, acetazolamide titrated up, short-term simple analgesia without opioids, and ophthalmology follow-up timed by the papilledema grade. Declining vision goes to urgent surgery.

Papilledema with an opening pressure of 25 cm CSF or less: below the IIH cut-off, so the picture is reread. An experienced clinician reviews the discs, and a repeat LP or intracranial pressure monitoring may be considered.

Carbon monoxide poisoning without severe signs: 100% oxygen until symptom-free with COHb below 3%, admission while symptomatic, ECG and troponin, the source found, and a warning about delayed neurological sequelae. A normal COHb does not exclude it when the exposure and symptoms fit.
Severe carbon monoxide poisoning: 100% oxygen, hyperbaric oxygen within 6 hours, cardiac monitoring, and a warning about delayed neurological sequelae.
Severe hypertension without acute target organ damage: no aggressive short-term lowering, no parenteral drugs; restart or intensify oral therapy.
Orthostatic headache: the ACR rates MRI head without and with IV contrast usually appropriate, CT usually not (Variant 5); the rest is outside this pathway's sources.

Hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy: ICU, a titratable IV agent, systolic down by no more than 25% in the first hour, then below 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours and 130 to 140 over the next 24 to 48 hours.

Imaging clear after a secondary-cause red flag: no bleed, mass or abscess. Over 50, giant cell arteritis is still possible; the rest of the workup for cancer or compromised immunity is outside this pathway's sources.

New hypertension with proteinuria in pregnancy or after delivery: possible pre-eclampsia. Hand over to the obstetric team now. A systolic of 160 or more or a diastolic of 110 or more is severe-range and is treated urgently (AHA/ACC 2025); its agent and dose table is reprinted from ACOG and is not shown here. Magnesium and delivery timing are outside this pathway's sources.

Migraine in the ED: IV metoclopramide or prochlorperazine with an IV NSAID, sumatriptan SC if the pain persists and nothing rules it out, no opioids or ergots, and no imaging for reassurance. Whether to add dexamethasone against recurrence is not settled by the full texts read.
Tension-type headache: aspirin, acetaminophen or an NSAID, no opioids, no imaging for reassurance, and a warning about medication overuse.
Medication overuse headache: stop all overused acute drugs abruptly for at least 1 month, expect a worse spell first, consider prophylaxis for the underlying headache, and review in 4 to 8 weeks.

Cluster headache: 100% oxygen at 12 L/min or more by non-rebreather and/or sumatriptan 6 mg SC; no oral triptans, NSAIDs or opioids; verapamil for the bout with specialist advice; home oxygen; neuroimaging discussed for a first bout.

cases.label: Thunderclap, blood on the CT
cases.vignette: 52-year-old woman, a sudden severe headache that peaked within a minute while she lifted a box 2 hours ago, then vomiting and neck pain. BP 168/94, HR 88, temperature 36.9.

results.front_door: Peak within a minute, 2 hours ago. GCS 15, no focal deficit, no fever; neck stiff on flexion.
results.sah_ct_result: Non-contrast CT at 2.5 hours: blood in the basal cisterns and both sylvian fissures.
results.cta_result: CT angiography: a 7 mm posterior communicating artery aneurysm; the blood pattern fits its rupture.
